beginner: Rosemary likes poor, dry, gritty soil and full sun. Rich, damp soil and heavy clay make it weak and rot-prone, so the goal is fast drainage, not fertility. If your soil is heavy, plant rosemary on a mound or raised bed and mix in coarse sand or grit so water drains straight through.

On clay, plant on a raised bed or mound and add coarse material rather than piling on rich compost.

beginner: The trick with rosemary is to not overwater it and to give it your sunniest, best-draining spot. Water deeply but only once in a while, and skip the fertilizer. beginner: The easy, reliable way to grow rosemary is to buy a small plant or take a cutting from an existing one. Growing it from seed is slow and unpredictable, and seed-grown plants often do not match the parent, so most gardeners skip it. If you do want to try seed, surface-sow it and do not cover it, since the seed needs light to sprout, keep it warm around 70°F, and start indoors about 10 weeks before your last frost; expect slow, uneven germination.
seasoned: Rosemary is almost always started from a nursery transplant or from stem cuttings, not from seed. Seed germinates slowly and unevenly and can take about three years to reach a mature plant, and named cultivars do not come true from seed, so growers propagate them from cuttings. Take tip cuttings a few inches long, root them with warmth (bottom heat around 70 to 75°F), and they root in a couple of weeks. To grow from seed instead, surface-sow at about 70°F since the seed needs light, starting indoors roughly 10 weeks before the last frost; germination is slow and uneven and the seedlings size up gradually, which is why most growers still choose cuttings.

For cooking, any of the upright green-needled types work well; for a container or a wall, choose a trailing form.

beginner: Rosemary is an evergreen shrubby herb with fragrant, needle-like leaves and small blue flowers. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it loves sun and hates wet feet. You grow it mostly for the leaves, which you can snip year round in mild climates. It is less cold hardy than sage or thyme: it lives outdoors year after year only in warmer areas (about zone 7 or 8 and up), and in cold-winter places most people grow it in a pot and bring it inside for the winter. Give it full sun, fast-draining soil, and go easy on the water, since too much water is the fastest way to kill it.
seasoned: Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) is a woody evergreen Mediterranean subshrub in the mint family, grown mainly for its aromatic, needle-like culinary leaves and secondarily for its small blue flowers. It comes in upright forms that reach several feet and low trailing forms that spill over walls. Unlike hardier culinary perennials such as sage and thyme, rosemary is relatively cold tender: it is reliably perennial only in mild zones (roughly zone 7 or 8 and warmer, with the hardy cultivar Arp pushing into zone 6), and in colder regions it is grown as an annual or overwintered indoors in a pot. It wants full sun, lean sharply drained soil, and little water; overwatering and wet, poorly drained soil, not cold alone, are its most common killers.

beginner: You grow rosemary for the leaves, and in mild areas you can snip sprigs almost any time of year. For the best flavor, cut sprigs from the soft green growth in the morning, especially just before it flowers. Snip stems just above a leafy joint so the plant grows back bushy, and take no more than about a fifth of the plant at once. To dry it, cut sprigs before or during flowering, hang small bunches somewhere warm and airy, and strip the leaves off once they are dry.
seasoned: Rosemary is grown for its leaves, and in mild climates you can snip fresh sprigs almost year round. For drying, cut sprigs before or at flowering, then hang them in small bundles in a warm, airy place and strip the leaves once dry.

beginner: Rosemary is less cold hardy than most herbs. In colder places, grow rosemary in a pot and bring it inside for the winter, since it will not survive a hard freeze in the ground the way sage or thyme can.
seasoned: Rosemary is relatively cold tender for a woody herb. Below that, in roughly zone 6 and colder, rosemary is grown as an annual or, better, kept in a container and moved to a bright, cool, protected place for winter. This is the opposite of hardier culinary perennials like sage and thyme, which overwinter outdoors much farther north.
